snippets.text: What if I told you there's a way to
access cash from your portfolio without
selling a single share and without
paying a dollar in capital gains tax?
This is not a loophole. This is how the
ultra-wealthy have been doing it for
decades. And recently, I started doing
this myself. So, today I'm going to
break down the full strategy, what it
is, how I personally set it up, and the
stuff that nobody tells you about the
risks. So, you've probably heard those
headlines, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, some
billionaire made $5 billion last year
and paid almost nothing in taxes. And
you're sitting there thinking, how is
that even legal? And probably, I want to
do that, too.
I used to think the same thing. And the
answer is something called buy, borrow,
die.
And once you understand how this
actually works, and I mean really
understand it, I transferred a
significant chunk of my portfolio to
make it happen. So, let me explain this.
Here's the core idea. You buy assets,
stocks, ETFs, mutual funds, and you hold
them. You don't sell them. Instead of
selling, you borrow against them. The
assets sit in your account, they
continue to grow, and you pay interest
on whatever you borrow. That borrowed
money is not a taxable event. You're not
realizing a gain, you're taking a loan.
So, you're living off borrowed cash
while your portfolio quietly compounds
in the background. Now, here's the part
that tripped me up for a long time.
Yeah, but at some point you have to pay
the loan back, right?
And here's the answer. Yes, you do. But
there's a key insight that I was
missing. Because you're never selling,
that portfolio keeps growing. A few
years go by, your assets are worth more
than when you took the initial loan out.
Then you take out a new loan at the
higher value, and you use that to pay
off the old one, and you just keep
rotating. That's the machine. And the
die part of this, which is the final
piece, when you eventually pass away,
those assets go to your family, your
heirs inherit them at the current market
value, and not at your original cost
basis. That step-up in basis effectively
wipes out capital gains that built up
over your lifetime. And that's the full
picture. Buy assets, borrow against
them, and pass them on. Now, let me get
into exactly how I did this, because
this is where it gets real. As my
portfolio has grown, taxes have become
my number one financial problem. I was
selling roughly $60,000 a year to cover
expenses, and every single dollar of
that was a taxable event for me. And
when I got hit with that tax bill last
year, the biggest one of my life,
something clicked. I said, I am done
selling. So, instead of selling, I'm now
borrowing. I pay interest on the
borrowed amount, my assets continue to
grow, and in a few years, I'm going to
rotate the loan. Now, this strategy
really only makes sense at a certain
scale. I'd say you need $500,000,
minimum $100,000,
in a portfolio of long-term holdings
you're not actively trading. So, we're
talking about ETFs, index funds, maybe
some blue-chip positions you plan to
hold for the long haul. But, if you're
actively trading in and out, this
becomes a lot more complicated and a lot
harder to manage. So, after shopping
around, Interactive Brokers offered the
best borrowing rate I could find
anywhere. Now, IBKR offers two versions.
There's IBKR Lite and IBKR Pro. IBKR
Lite is free commissions. It's a lighter
platform and simpler experience. IBKR
Pro gives you a near institutional level
trading platform and a significantly
lower margin rate. But, you pay
commissions on your trades. But, because
this is a long-term buy and hold
portfolio, I went with IBKR Pro purely
for the lower rates.
And here's how the current rate
structure actually works, and this is
important. They don't charge one flat
rate. They use a tiered system. On the
first $100,000 you borrow, the current
rate is 5.12%.
Borrow between 100,000 and a million,
that drops to 4.62%.
Above a million, you're looking at
roughly 4.37%.
So, if you're borrowing a meaningful
amount, your blended rate is
meaningfully lower than that first tier
number. Compare that to what most
traditional brokerages charge, some are
running 8 to 10% on comparable balances.
IBKR is less than half the cost. That
difference matters a lot when you're
talking about a multi-year loan. Now, I
want to be honest about something here.
What I originally was looking for was a
securities backed line of credit, a
dedicated structured credit facility
like what private banks offer their high
net worth clients. I couldn't actually
find one with a decent rate that was
accessible at my portfolio size. So,
what Interactive Brokers offers instead
is a margin account. A margin account is
a brokerage account that allows you to
borrow money from the broker using your
portfolio as collateral. And here's what
makes it different from a traditional
loan. There's no application, there's no
credit check, there's no fixed repayment
schedule. When your cash balance goes
negative, that's your loan. That's how
simple it is. You hold $100,000 in ETFs,
you pull out 30,000 in cash, your
account now shows a negative $30,000
cash balance, and that's your margin
loan. Interest accrues daily, posts
monthly, and floats with short-term Fed
benchmark rates.
Interactive Brokers requires 50% initial
margin, meaning you need at least $2 in
portfolio value for every dollar you
borrow to start. The maintenance margin
is 25%. That's the floor you cannot fall
below. If your portfolio drops enough
that your equity dips under that 25%
threshold, Interactive Brokers does not
call you. They don't give you a warning
window to deposit more cash, they
liquidate your positions automatically.
And that's the most important thing to
understand about the strategy. It's not
a traditional line of credit. It's
margin. And if the market drops hard and
fast, your broker will sell the holdings
for you at whatever price they can get
before you even pick up the phone.
That's why sizing matters enormously.
Now, I'm not borrowing anywhere near the
maximum that the account allows. If your
portfolio is worth $1 million, they
might technically let you borrow
500,000, but I would not do that. When
you're running this as a long-term
wealth strategy, you want a significant
cushion. Enough that even a 30 or 40%
market correction doesn't push you
anywhere near that maintenance
threshold. The sweet spot most people
talk about is borrowing no more than 10
to 20% of your portfolio value. That
keeps you safe through normal market
volatility and gives you room to
breathe. So, let me walk you through a
simple example because the numbers need
to make sense. Say you have a
million-dollar portfolio, mostly broad
ETFs like the SPY or QQQ. You borrow
$100,000 at roughly 4.6% interest.
That's approximately $4,600
per year in interest. Your portfolio
historically returns somewhere around 7
to 10% annualized. On a million dollars,
7% is 70,000. You're paying 4,600 in
interest to keep that million working
for you rather than selling a chunk of
it and locking in a capital gains bill.
And here's the compounding angle. That
100,000 you didn't sell is still in the
market, still growing, and still
compounding. At 7% over 5 years,
The loan doesn't grow, but the
collateral does. And that is the whole
game. So, I want to be completely
straight with you on the risks because
this strategy is not for everyone, and
it can go sideways fast if you are not
careful. Risk number one is going to be
the forced liquidation. I already
mentioned this, but it bears repeating.
Interactive Brokers will liquidate your
positions immediately if your equity
drops below the maintenance margin.
There's no warning, no grace period.
This is not a bank, it's a brokerage.
Risk number two is going to be interest
costs in a flat or down market. If your
portfolio stagnates or falls while
you're carrying a loan, you're paying
interest on borrowed money against
assets that are not growing. The math
only works when your portfolio return
exceeds your borrowing costs over time.
And risk number three is this is a long
game. This is not a strategy you run on
a concentrated actively traded
portfolio. It requires stable,
diversified, long-term holdings. The
minute you start actively moving in and
out of positions, you introduce timing
risk that can blow up the whole
structure. And risk number four is going
to be tax complexity. The interest you
pay may or may not be tax deductible
depending on your situation. This is
where a CPA or someone who understands
investment interest expenses becomes
valuable. Don't skip that conversation,
but I'm not that person. So, here's the
bottom line. The wealthy don't get rich
by selling their assets every time they
need cash. They build, they borrow, and
they let time do the work. This strategy
is not new, but the access to it has
never been cheaper or more available to
regular investors than it is right now.
And personally, I'm still figuring this
out myself. This is something I just
started, but I'm going to keep
documenting the journey on this channel.
The rates, the loan structure, how I'm
sizing it, and how the strategy evolves.
If you want to follow along, hit
subscribe and turn on notifications. And
drop a comment. Are you currently
borrowing against your portfolio, or is
this something you consider? I'm
genuinely curious where you all are on
this. This is not financial advice,
always do your own research before
investing. I'm not a financial advisor,
just someone teaching my personal
finance in public.
